narrative:
The model estimated a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your application was denied because the decision treated that risk as too high. This is a probability, not a certainty: it means the model judged failure more likely than passing based on your record.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. Your third-year decile was 2, well below the average of about 5.8 among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score of 39, slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37.2; this was the major factor working in your favor and pushed toward passing. The third most important factor was your first-year decile of 3, compared with an accepted-student average of 6, which also pushed toward failure. Together, the two low class-standing indicators outweighed the positive LSAT signal.

Your gender and race were not used in the prediction. To proceed, ask admissions for a review and clarification, especially whether you can submit updated academic evidence or a statement explaining your early academic record. Consider meeting with an advisor about strengthening your profile, delaying reapplication until you have stronger recent grades, and documenting any circumstances that affected your performance.
